Your website looks professional. So why isn’t it creating opportunities?

Most Florida businesses we meet don’t have a design problem. They have a system problem.

The website was built by one company, the SEO is handled by another, the ads by a third — and nobody owns the one number that matters: how many qualified customers reach out each month.

Symptom 1

Traffic without calls.

People visit, look around and leave. The site answers “who we are” but not “why you, why now.”

Symptom 2

Invisible where it counts.

Competitors show up in the map pack and on page one for the searches your best customers actually make.

Symptom 3

Paying for leads you don’t own.

Referral sites and lead marketplaces fill the gap, at a price that grows every season.

01 Approach

Growth is a system, not a set of tactics.

Before anything gets built, we find out where your growth is actually stuck. Then every piece — website, search, campaigns, tracking — is designed to work toward the same goal.

  1. 01

    Research

    Your market, your competitors, and how customers in your area search, compare and decide.

  2. 02

    Strategy

    Positioning, offer and priorities. What to do first, and what to ignore.

  3. 03

    Digital System

    Website, local search, campaigns and tracking, built to work together.

  4. 04

    Growth

    Measure qualified opportunities, learn, improve — every month.

Questions owners ask

Do you only work with Florida businesses?
My focus is Southwest Florida — Fort Myers, Naples, Cape Coral and nearby — because local knowledge is part of the value. I also work with select businesses elsewhere in Florida and internationally.
Can you guarantee first-page rankings?
No one honestly can. What I can promise is a clear strategy, solid execution and transparent reporting on the numbers that matter: calls, requests and booked jobs.
How long until we see results?
Website and conversion improvements can show impact within weeks. Local SEO typically builds over 3–6 months, depending on competition and your starting point.
Do I need a new website?
Not always. The audit tells us whether to rebuild, improve or leave it alone.
Who actually does the work?
I lead strategy and stay involved throughout. Design, development and campaigns are delivered by my team at HelloProVision.

01 Story

An entrepreneur first

02 Florida

A European perspective, built for Florida

[Verified: when and why you moved to Florida, and what you’ve built here since.]

Working across markets taught me something useful: the fundamentals of growth travel well, but the details never do. How a homeowner in Naples chooses a contractor is different from how a business buyer in Budapest chooses a partner. Good strategy starts with that local reality — who your customers are, how they search, and what makes them trust someone.

Southwest Florida is a remarkable place to build a business: fast population growth, seasonal rhythms, a premium market and fierce local competition. It rewards businesses that are easy to find, easy to trust and easy to contact. That’s exactly what I help build.

03 Principles

How I think about growth

  • Strategy means choosing.

    If everything is a priority, nothing is. Good strategy says what to do first — and what not to do yet.

  • Numbers need context.

    I start from data, but a metric rarely explains itself. I connect the numbers to your customers, your team and your decisions.

  • A plan you can execute beats a perfect plan.

    Recommendations have to fit your budget, your people and your pace.

  • Technology is a tool, not a strategy.

    Websites, SEO, ads and AI matter only when they solve a clear business problem.

04 Focus

What I focus on

My core work is digital growth strategy for established Florida businesses, supported by three disciplines: strategic website design and development, local SEO and search growth, and conversion-focused digital marketing. When something falls outside what I do best, I’ll tell you — and point you to someone who does it better.

Accessibility statement

Last updated: [launch date]

I want every business owner to be able to use this website, including people who use screen readers, keyboard navigation, magnification or other assistive technology.

The standard we follow

This site is designed and tested to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, level AA. In practice that means:

  • Text contrast of at least 4.5:1 against its background
  • Visible focus states and full keyboard access for menus, forms and accordions
  • Tap targets of at least 44 × 44 pixels
  • Headings in a logical order and descriptive link text
  • Alternative text for meaningful images
  • Form fields with visible labels and clear error messages
  • Animation turned off when your device asks for reduced motion

Known limitations

Third-party tools, such as the booking calendar, are provided by other companies. We choose tools with good accessibility, but can’t fully control them. If one gets in your way, contact me and I’ll book the call for you directly.

Report a problem

If something on this site is hard to use, please tell me. I aim to reply within two business days.

    Websites · 6 min read

    Why your website gets traffic but no calls

    Your analytics show visitors. Your phone doesn’t ring. The gap between the two is almost never the design — it’s five small decisions about what a visitor sees, believes and can do next.

    Áron Ritók-Filip

    Digital Growth Strategist · September 24, 2026

    Most owners who tell me “the website isn’t working” are looking at the wrong problem. Traffic is there: people search, click and land. Then they leave. They didn’t hate the site. It just never gave them a reason to act today, with you, rather than the next result on the page.

    If this sounds familiar, the fix is usually not a new logo or a new template. It’s the way the site is built to sell — which is what I mean when I talk about treating a website as a digital sales system. Here are the five places interested visitors most often give up.

    1. The first screen answers the wrong question

    Most homepages open with who the company is: “Family-owned since…”, “Quality craftsmanship…”. A visitor who just searched “kitchen remodeler Fort Myers” is asking something else: can you do my job, in my area, at the level I want?

    The first screen should answer that in one sentence, name the area you serve and show one clear next step. If a visitor has to scroll to find out what you do, many won’t.

    2. Proof is hidden where nobody looks

    Reviews live on a separate page. Project photos sit in a gallery with no context. Yet proof matters most at the moment of doubt: next to the price question, next to the contact form, right under the headline.

    Put one strong project and one real review on every page that asks for a call. A named customer from a nearby city outweighs ten anonymous five-star quotes.

    3. Every service shares one page

    If your pool resurfacing, new builds and repairs share a single “Services” page, you’re invisible for most of the searches your customers actually make — and the visitors who do arrive have to dig for the part that matters to them.

    Each high-value service deserves its own page: what it includes, who it’s for, a relevant project and a way to ask about it. That page is both what ranks and what converts.

    4. Contacting you takes work

    Many local customers decide on a phone, often in between other things. Test your own site on a phone:

    • Is the phone number tappable from every page, without scrolling?
    • Does the contact form fit on one screen, with only the fields you really need?
    • Does the visitor know what happens after they submit — and how fast?

    Each extra step loses people who were ready to talk.

    5. Nobody knows which visits turn into jobs

    Without call tracking and form tracking, you can’t tell which pages and searches bring customers, so every change is a guess. The goal isn’t more traffic reports. It’s one number you trust: qualified opportunities per month, and where they came from.

    Where to start

    Fix them in this order: the first screen, proof placement, contact on mobile, then service pages, then tracking. The first three are often a few days of work and can change results within weeks. Service pages and tracking take longer, and they are also what local SEO builds on.

    If you’d like a second pair of eyes, the Digital Growth Scorecard takes five minutes and shows which of these areas is holding you back most.
